patterns.usage_note: The everyday marker for a result that contradicts what the first clause led you to expect, usually coloured with dissatisfaction, regret or surprise; the first clause states something already established, not a hypothesis. It is neutral about who the subjects are, so it covers ground くせに cannot: くせに needs one shared, criticizable person, while のに happily contrasts two different subjects or none at all. After a noun or na-adjective it needs な (まだ四月なのに), and left dangling at the end of a sentence it becomes a sigh of regret (来てくれればよかったのに).

examples.ruby: 部屋[へや]はこんなに寒[さむ]いのに、弟[おとうと]は窓[まど]を開[あ]けたがる。
examples.english: The room is freezing, and yet my little brother keeps wanting to open the window.

examples.ruby: 毎日[まいにち]水[みず]をやるのに、この鉢[はち]の花[はな]は咲[さ]かない。
examples.english: I water it every day, and still the flowers in this pot won't bloom.

examples.ruby: 約束[やくそく]の時間[じかん]を過[す]ぎたのに、電車[でんしゃ]はまだ来[こ]ない。
examples.english: The scheduled time has come and gone, and the train still isn't here.

glosses: when all it would have taken was …
patterns.usage_note: Formal noun もの plus を, used to voice exasperation or regret that an easy better course was not taken; it typically follows a conditional (〜ば / 〜たら … ものを) and very often ends the sentence, leaving the actual outcome unspoken and the complaint hanging. It is stiffer and more emotionally loaded than のに, which can report a plain contradiction with no blame attached; もんを is its spoken contraction. It also attaches to i-adjectives, most often in the fixed frame 〜ばいいものを (黙っていればいいものを).

examples.ruby: 素直[すなお]に謝[あやま]れば済[す]むものを、彼[かれ]は言[い]い訳[わけ]を並[なら]べた。
examples.english: A simple apology would have settled it, and instead he reeled off excuses.

examples.ruby: 一言[ひとこと]相談[そうだん]してくれれば、金[かね]の工面[くめん]はできるものを。
examples.english: If he'd said one word to me, I could have scared up the money.

examples.ruby: 早[はや]めに出[で]れば間[ま]に合[あ]うものを、妹[いもうと]はぎりぎりまで寝[ね]ていた。
examples.english: Leaving early would have got her there in time, and my sister lay in bed till the last second.

patterns.usage_note: Formal noun ところ plus を, marking a situation that the following clause then cuts against. Two uses share the form: prefacing a request, apology or thanks by naming the inconvenience being imposed (お忙しいところを恐れ入りますが), and pointing out a departure from the normal course of things (普段なら三十分で着くところを). It belongs to ceremonious speech and written narration, and the preceding clause is typically non-past. After a noun it takes の (お休みのところを).

examples.ruby: お忙[いそが]しいところを、わざわざお越[こ]しいただき恐縮[きょうしゅく]です。
examples.english: I'm much obliged to you for coming all this way when you're so busy.

examples.ruby: 普段[ふだん]なら三十分[さんじゅっぷん]で着[つ]くところを、二時間[にじかん]も要[よう]した。
examples.english: A trip that would normally take half an hour ended up taking two full hours.

examples.ruby: 実費[じっぴ]を請求[せいきゅう]できるところを、先方[せんぽう]は無償[むしょう]で応[おう]じた。
examples.english: They would have been within their rights to bill us for costs, yet they handled it free of charge.
